title: LangChain Building Blocks
summary: LangChain gives you standardized components — chat models, prompt templates, output parsers, and tools — plus LCEL, a pipe syntax that composes them into a runnable chain. Its value is a uniform interface across providers and reusable pieces, not magic; for a single call, raw SDK code is often clearer. LangChain handles the linear composition; LangGraph handles stateful, branching, and cyclic control flow, and the two interoperate.

subtopics.title: Chat models: one interface across providers
subtopics.explanation: A LangChain chat model wraps a provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, and others) behind a common interface, so .invoke(messages) returns a message object regardless of vendor. This lets you swap models by changing one line instead of rewriting call code. The uniform interface is the main reason to adopt LangChain — it decouples your logic from any single provider's SDK.
subtopics.example:
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
# swap to `from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic`
# without changing the code below

model = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0)
resp = model.invoke("Name one primary color.")
print(resp.content)   # same shape no matter the provider

subtopics.title: Prompt templates turn variables into messages
subtopics.explanation: A ChatPromptTemplate defines a reusable prompt with placeholders and produces a properly-structured list of messages when you fill them in. It separates prompt wording from call-site code and prevents ad-hoc f-string mistakes like unescaped braces or missing roles. Templating is what makes prompts versionable and testable, so they become an asset rather than scattered strings.
subtopics.example:
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", "You are a terse assistant."),
    ("human", "Translate '{text}' to {language}."),
])

messages = prompt.invoke({"text": "hello", "language": "French"})
# -> structured system + human messages, ready for a model

subtopics.title: Output parsers turn model text into usable data
subtopics.explanation: An output parser converts the model's message into the type your code needs: StrOutputParser for plain text, or structured parsers that validate JSON against a schema (often a pydantic model). Parsing lives at the end of a chain so the chain's final output is data, not a raw message object. This is the same 'structured output' discipline applied as a composable component you can reuse across chains.
subtopics.example:
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser

parser = StrOutputParser()
# turns an AIMessage into just its .content string
text = parser.invoke(model.invoke("Say hi in one word."))
print(text)   # 'Hi' -- a plain str, not a message object
# structured parsers can instead validate JSON into a schema

subtopics.title: Tools: functions the model can call
subtopics.explanation: LangChain wraps a Python function as a tool (via the @tool decorator or a schema) and lets you bind tools to a model so it can emit tool calls; your code executes them and feeds results back. The framework standardizes the tool schema and the call/response format across providers. Tools are how a LangChain-powered model reaches the outside world, and bound tools are the raw material an agent loop iterates over.
subtopics.example:
from langchain_core.tools import tool

@tool
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two integers."""   # docstring becomes the description
    return a + b

model_with_tools = model.bind_tools([add])
resp = model_with_tools.invoke("What is 2 + 3?")
# resp.tool_calls -> [{'name': 'add', 'args': {'a': 2, 'b': 3}, ...}]

subtopics.title: LCEL composes pieces with the pipe operator
subtopics.explanation: LangChain Expression Language (LCEL) uses | to wire components into a single Runnable: prompt | model | parser reads left to right, each stage feeding the next, and the whole thing gets .invoke/.stream/.batch for free. It is great for linear pipelines but deliberately not for branching, loops, or shared state — that is LangGraph's job. Knowing this boundary tells you when to compose with LCEL and when to reach for a graph.
subtopics.example:
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser

chain = prompt | model | StrOutputParser()   # a Runnable

# .invoke, .stream, .batch all come for free
out = chain.invoke({"text": "hello", "language": "French"})
print(out)          # 'Bonjour' (a plain string)
# for loops/branches/state, wrap chains as nodes in LangGraph

foundations.overview: LangChain is a toolkit of standardized components for building LLM applications, plus a composition layer to wire them together. The core components are: chat models, which wrap any provider behind one .invoke interface so you can swap vendors trivially; prompt templates, which turn variables into correctly-structured message lists and make prompts reusable and testable; output parsers, which convert a model's message into the string or validated structured data your code needs; and tools, ordinary Python functions wrapped with a schema and bound to a model so it can request calls your code executes. The composition layer is LCEL, the LangChain Expression Language, where the pipe operator chains components — prompt | model | parser — into a single Runnable that automatically supports invoke, stream, and batch. The honest framing matters: LangChain's value is the uniform interface and reusable building blocks, not hidden intelligence. For a single provider call, the raw SDK is often shorter and clearer; LangChain pays off when you want provider portability, standardized tools/parsers, and composable pipelines. Crucially, LCEL is built for linear composition — it does not do branching, loops, or shared state. That is where LangGraph takes over, and the two interoperate cleanly: a LangChain chain (a Runnable) drops straight into a LangGraph node, so you use LangChain for the pieces and LangGraph for stateful control flow.
foundations.formalDefinition: LangChain defines a set of Runnable components (chat models, prompt templates, output parsers, tools) sharing a common interface (invoke/stream/batch). LCEL composes Runnables with the | operator into a new Runnable whose output of stage n is the input of stage n+1. A tool is a callable exposed to a model via a schema; bind_tools attaches tool schemas so the model can emit structured tool calls. LangChain chains are Runnables and can therefore be used directly as nodes inside a LangGraph.
foundations.whyItMatters: Teams need to avoid rewriting prompt handling, parsing, tool schemas, and provider glue for every project and every vendor. LangChain standardizes these so they become swappable, testable parts — and its clean interop with LangGraph means you can assemble linear pieces with LCEL and reach for a graph only when you need state and control flow, without changing tools or models.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of LangChain as a set of standardized electrical components — plugs, switches, adapters — that all fit the same sockets, and LCEL as the wire that snaps them into a line. You get portability and reuse, but the wire only runs straight; when you need junctions, loops, and memory in the circuit, you install a LangGraph control board and plug the same components into it.
foundations.realWorldUsage: LCEL chains power retrieval-augmented pipelines (prompt | model | parser over retrieved context), classification and extraction chains with structured parsers, and provider-agnostic services that swap models via config. Tools and bind_tools underpin function-calling features, while the LangChain-in-LangGraph pattern builds full agents where each graph node is a LangChain chain.
foundations.performanceImpact: Component overhead is negligible against LLM latency; LCEL adds value here by giving .batch (concurrent inputs) and .stream for free, which improve throughput and perceived latency. The main cost consideration is not the framework but the same LLM levers as always — model choice, temperature, and prompt size.
commonUseCases: Provider-agnostic services that swap models with one line
RAG and extraction pipelines composed as prompt | model | parser
LangChain chains used as nodes inside a LangGraph agent

commonMisconceptions.myth: LangChain is required to call an LLM.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's optional. For a single call the provider SDK is often clearer; LangChain earns its place through portability, reusable components, and composition, not necessity.

commonMisconceptions.myth: LCEL can express loops, branches, and stateful agents.
commonMisconceptions.reality: LCEL is for linear composition. Branching, cycles, and shared state are LangGraph's domain — that's why the two are separate tools that interoperate.

commonMisconceptions.myth: LangChain and LangGraph are competing choices.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They're complementary: LangChain provides the components and linear chains, LangGraph provides stateful control flow, and a LangChain chain plugs directly into a LangGraph node.

interactiveExamples.title: A basic LCEL chain: prompt | model | parser
interactiveExamples.explanation: The canonical three-stage chain, shown with a fake model so it runs deterministically. The prompt fills variables into messages, the model produces a message, and StrOutputParser extracts the plain string — and the whole chain is one Runnable.

code.code:
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", "You are terse."),
    ("human", "Greet {name}."),
])

# a fake 'model': a Runnable that echoes a canned reply
fake_model = RunnableLambda(lambda msgs: "Hello, Ada!")

chain = prompt | fake_model | StrOutputParser()
print(chain.invoke({"name": "Ada"}))
code.caption: prompt | model | parser is a single Runnable; a RunnableLambda stands in for a real chat model so the pipeline is deterministic.

interactiveExamples.title: Defining a tool and inspecting its generated schema
interactiveExamples.explanation: The @tool decorator turns a typed, documented function into a LangChain tool, deriving the name, description, and argument schema automatically — exactly what bind_tools sends to the model. Here we call the tool directly and read its schema without needing a live model.

code.caption: The function's signature and docstring become the tool's schema and description — the contract a model uses to emit a valid tool call.
code.expectedOutput:
word_count
Count the words in a piece of text.
{'text': {'title': 'Text', 'type': 'string'}}
3

codeLab.title: Build a reusable LCEL classification chain
codeLab.instructions: Complete build_chain(fake_model) so it returns an LCEL chain of prompt | fake_model | StrOutputParser that classifies a ticket. The prompt must have a system message telling the model to reply with exactly one lowercase word from 'billing', 'technical', or 'other', and a human message containing the '{ticket}' variable. Compose the three stages with the pipe operator and return the resulting Runnable. The fake_model and parser wiring are what you assemble; the test passes a stub model that returns 'billing'.

starter.code:
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser

def build_chain(fake_model):
    # TODO: build a ChatPromptTemplate with a system rule and a
    #       human message using {ticket}, then compose
    #       prompt | fake_model | StrOutputParser() and return it.
    ...

solution.code:
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser

def build_chain(fake_model):
    prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
        ("system",
         "Classify the support ticket. Reply with exactly one "
         "lowercase word: billing, technical, or other."),
        ("human", "{ticket}"),
    ])
    # pipe the three Runnables into a single chain
    return prompt | fake_model | StrOutputParser()

codeLab.testHarness:
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda

# stub model: ignores input, returns a canned label
fake_model = RunnableLambda(lambda messages: "billing")

chain = build_chain(fake_model)
result = chain.invoke({"ticket": "I was charged twice this month"})
assert result == "billing", result
assert isinstance(result, str), type(result)
print("all tests passed")
hints: ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages takes a list of (role, template) tuples; use 'system' for the rule and 'human' for '{ticket}'.
The pipe operator | composes Runnables left to right: prompt feeds the model, the model feeds the parser.
StrOutputParser() at the end guarantees the chain's output is a plain string, not a message object.

debuggingLab.title: The chain returns a message object, and an f-string prompt breaks on braces
debuggingLab.symptom: Downstream code does result.lower() and crashes with AttributeError because the LCEL chain returns an AIMessage, not a string. Separately, building the prompt with an f-string that contains literal JSON braces raises a KeyError the moment the template is formatted.

brokenCode.code:
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate

# BUG 2: f-string interpolates now, and the literal { } in the JSON
# example collide with template variable syntax later
prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("human", f"Return JSON like {{'ok': true}} for: {topic}"),
])

# BUG 1: no output parser -> chain output is an AIMessage, not str
chain = prompt | model

msg = chain.invoke({"topic": "cats"})
print(msg.lower())   # AttributeError: AIMessage has no attribute 'lower'

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Two mistakes. First, the chain is prompt | model with no output parser, so its result is an AIMessage object; calling .lower() on it fails because string methods live on the message's .content, not the message. Second, the prompt is built with a Python f-string, which both interpolates {topic} too early (before it's a template variable) and mishandles the literal braces in the JSON example — in a LangChain template, real variables use single braces and literal braces must be doubled. The combination means the template either KeyErrors on format or embeds the wrong text. Use a plain template string (not an f-string), double any literal braces, and end the chain with StrOutputParser so the output is a usable string.
commonMistakes: Omitting an output parser and then treating the AIMessage as if it were a string (call .content or add StrOutputParser).
Using a Python f-string for a prompt template, which interpolates immediately and clashes with LangChain's {variable} syntax.
Forgetting to escape literal braces by doubling them ({{ }}), so JSON examples in the prompt are parsed as template variables.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Build the prompt as a normal template string with the variable as {topic} and literal JSON braces doubled ({{ }}), and append StrOutputParser() so the chain yields a plain string safe to call .lower() on.

solution.code:
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda

# plain template string: {topic} is a variable, {{ }} are literal braces
prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("human", "Return JSON like {{'ok': true}} for: {topic}"),
])

# stand-in model; a real ChatOpenAI/ChatAnthropic would return an AIMessage
model = RunnableLambda(lambda messages: '{"OK": true}')

# StrOutputParser makes the chain output a plain string
chain = prompt | model | StrOutputParser()

text = chain.invoke({"topic": "cats"})
print(text.lower())   # works: text is a str, not an AIMessage

checkpoints.prompt: What does the pipe operator do in an LCEL chain like `prompt | model | parser`?
options: Runs the three stages in parallel
Composes them into one Runnable where each stage's output feeds the next
Chooses the best of the three at runtime
checkpoints.explanation: LCEL's | composes Runnables left to right into a single Runnable: the prompt's output feeds the model, whose output feeds the parser. The composed chain gets invoke/stream/batch automatically.

checkpoints.prompt: When is LangChain's LCEL the WRONG tool, calling for LangGraph instead?
options: A simple prompt -> model -> string pipeline
A workflow with loops, branching, and shared state across steps
Swapping one model provider for another
checkpoints.explanation: LCEL is for linear composition. Loops, conditional branching, and shared/persisted state are LangGraph's domain; LangChain chains then plug into LangGraph nodes.

theory.question: What are LangChain's core building blocks, and what does LCEL add on top of them?
theory.directAnswer: The core blocks are chat models (a uniform .invoke interface across providers), prompt templates (variables into structured messages), output parsers (message into a string or validated data), and tools (Python functions wrapped with a schema and bound to a model). LCEL, the expression language, composes these with the pipe operator into a single Runnable — prompt | model | parser — that automatically supports invoke, stream, and batch. Its value is a standard interface and reusable, swappable pieces, not hidden intelligence.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A set of standardized, interoperable components plus a pipe-based composition layer for building linear LLM pipelines.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Without it, every project reimplements provider glue, prompt formatting, parsing, and tool schemas per vendor; standardizing them makes the parts portable and testable.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each component is a Runnable with a common interface; LCEL's | wires the output of one stage into the next, producing a composed Runnable. Models expose bind_tools to attach tool schemas, and parsers convert the final message into usable data.

theory.whyImportant: It lets teams swap providers with one line, reuse prompts/parsers/tools across projects, and get streaming/batching for free — the practical payoff of adopting the framework.
theory.realWorldExample: A support service builds classify = prompt | model | StrOutputParser and swaps ChatOpenAI for ChatAnthropic via config with no other code change, reusing the same prompt template and parser.

followUps.question: Is LangChain necessary to call an LLM?
followUps.answer: No. For a single call the provider SDK is often clearer; LangChain pays off with portability, reusable components, and composition, not for one-off calls.

followUps.question: What does bind_tools actually do?
followUps.answer: It attaches the tools' JSON schemas to the model so it can emit structured tool calls; your code still executes the chosen function and feeds the result back.

theory.question: How do LangChain and LangGraph relate, and when do you use each?
theory.directAnswer: They're complementary. LangChain provides the components and LCEL for linear composition — great for prompt | model | parser pipelines, batching, and provider portability. LangGraph provides stateful control flow: branching, loops/cycles, shared typed state, persistence, and human-in-the-loop. Use LCEL when the flow is a straight line; reach for LangGraph when you need conditional paths, iteration, or memory across steps. They interoperate because a LangChain chain is a Runnable that plugs directly into a LangGraph node.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A division of labor: LangChain for reusable components and linear chains, LangGraph for the graph-shaped, stateful orchestration around them.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: LCEL deliberately doesn't model branches, cycles, or state to stay simple; LangGraph fills that gap, and keeping them separate lets each stay focused.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You build the pieces (prompt, model, tools, parser) and compose linear segments with LCEL, then embed those chains as node functions in a LangGraph whose edges and state handle branching, looping, and persistence.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the right layer avoids two common failures — bending LCEL into fragile branching hacks, or over-engineering a straight pipeline into a graph — and shows you understand where each tool's strengths lie.
theory.realWorldExample: An agent uses a LangChain chain (prompt | model.bind_tools | parser) as its 'reason' node inside a LangGraph tool-calling loop, so LangChain handles the call and LangGraph handles the cycle and state.

followUps.question: Can you build an agent loop in pure LCEL?
followUps.answer: Not cleanly — loops and conditional routing aren't what LCEL expresses; you'd use LangGraph for the cyclic, stateful loop and LCEL for the per-step chain.

followUps.question: Does mixing them require rewriting components?
followUps.answer: No — a LangChain Runnable drops into a LangGraph node as-is, so the same models, prompts, tools, and parsers carry over.

scenario.question: Your team wrote a bespoke wrapper around one provider's SDK; now product wants provider portability, structured extraction, and eventually a multi-step agent. How would you evolve the design using LangChain and LangGraph?
scenario.directAnswer: Adopt LangChain's chat-model abstraction so switching providers is a one-line config change, express the extraction as an LCEL chain (prompt | model | structured parser/pydantic) for portability and reuse, and standardize any external calls as @tool functions. When the requirement grows to multi-step with branching, loops, or memory, keep those LCEL chains as nodes inside a LangGraph that owns the state and control flow — evolving without rewriting the components.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A migration from a single-provider wrapper to standardized, composable components that scale into a stateful agent.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Bespoke wrappers lock you to one vendor and reimplement parsing/tooling; the requirements (portability, extraction, later agents) map directly onto LangChain components and LangGraph orchestration.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Replace direct SDK calls with a LangChain chat model, move prompts into templates, add a structured output parser for extraction, wrap side-effecting calls as tools, and compose with LCEL. For the agent phase, embed these chains as LangGraph nodes and use edges/state for the loop and memory.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows a pragmatic, incremental path that reuses each piece as requirements grow, rather than a rewrite — the realistic way frameworks earn adoption on a team.
scenario.realWorldExample: The team ships portability first (swap providers by config), then a pydantic-validated extraction chain, and finally a LangGraph tool-calling agent that reuses the very same chains as nodes.

followUps.question: Where might LangChain be overkill?
followUps.answer: If they'll only ever use one provider for one simple call, the raw SDK is clearer; the framework's benefits accrue with portability, reuse, and composition.

followUps.question: Why not jump straight to LangGraph for everything?
followUps.answer: Linear steps are simpler and clearer as LCEL chains; introduce the graph only when branching, loops, or shared state actually appear.

coding.question: Define a LangChain tool with @tool and write a function that, given a model's tool_calls, dispatches to the right tool and returns its result. Use a fake tool_calls list so it runs without a live model.
coding.thoughtProcess: The @tool decorator gives me a tool with a .name and an .invoke that runs the function on an args dict. I build a registry mapping tool name to the tool object, then iterate the model's tool_calls, look each up by name, and invoke it with its args — mirroring the execute step of an agent loop. I use a hand-built tool_calls list so no real model is needed.
lineByLine: @tool wraps each function into a tool with a name, description, and arg schema derived from the signature and docstring.
TOOLS is a registry mapping each tool's .name to the tool object for O(1) dispatch.
run_tool_calls iterates the model-emitted tool_calls, each a dict with 'name' and 'args'.
It looks up the tool by name and calls .invoke(args), which runs the underlying function on the argument dict.
The __main__ block hand-builds the tool_calls shape bind_tools would produce, so it runs with no live model and returns [42, 'DONE'].
coding.timeComplexity: O(k) for k tool calls, each an O(1) registry lookup plus the tool's own runtime.

followUps.question: How would this plug into a real agent loop?
followUps.answer: Call model.bind_tools([...]).invoke(messages), pass resp.tool_calls to run_tool_calls, append the results as tool messages, and loop until the model stops requesting tools.

followUps.question: Where would LangGraph fit here?
followUps.answer: The loop (model -> tools -> model until done) is cyclic and stateful, so you'd model it as a LangGraph with a conditional edge, using this dispatch inside the tools node.

keyTakeaways: LangChain's building blocks are chat models (uniform interface), prompt templates, output parsers, and tools — standardized, swappable, reusable pieces.
LCEL composes components with the pipe operator into one Runnable (prompt | model | parser) that gets invoke/stream/batch for free.
The value is portability and reuse, not magic — for a single call the raw provider SDK is often clearer.
LCEL is for linear composition only; branching, loops, and shared state belong to LangGraph.
LangChain and LangGraph are complementary: a LangChain chain is a Runnable that plugs directly into a LangGraph node, so you reuse the same components as needs grow.
